chapter_title: Creating and Updating Graph Data (CREATE, MERGE, SET, REMOVE)
chapter_summary:
Now that you're comfortable with retrieving data using `MATCH` and `RETURN`, it's time to learn how to change your graph. This chapter covers the essential Cypher clauses for data manipulation: `CREATE`, `MERGE`, `SET`, and `REMOVE`. These are your tools for building and evolving your graph database.

The `CREATE` clause is straightforward and is used to add new nodes and relationships to your graph. When you `CREATE` a node, you can specify its label(s) and initial properties. For example, to add a new `Person` node:
`CREATE (p:Person {name: 'Jane Doe', born: 1990}) RETURN p`
This query creates a new node, assigns it the `Person` label, sets its `name` and `born` properties, and then returns the newly created node. You can also create relationships between existing nodes or between newly created nodes. To create a new `Movie` and a `Person` who `DIRECTED` it:
```cypher
CREATE (m:Movie {title: 'New Sci-Fi', releaseYear: 2024})
CREATE (d:Person {name: 'Ava Director'})
CREATE (d)-[:DIRECTED]->(m)
RETURN m, d
```
It's important to note that `CREATE` will always create new entities, even if identical nodes or relationships already exist. This can lead to duplicate data if not used carefully.

This is where `MERGE` becomes incredibly powerful. The `MERGE` clause is designed for idempotent operations – it either matches an existing pattern in the graph or creates it if it doesn't already exist. This prevents the creation of duplicate data when you're unsure if a specific node or relationship already exists. For instance, if you want to ensure there's a `Person` named 'John Doe', but only create them if they don't exist:
`MERGE (p:Person {name: 'John Doe'}) RETURN p`
If a `Person` node with `name: 'John Doe'` already exists, `MERGE` will find and return it. If not, it will create it. `MERGE` can also be used for relationships. To ensure 'John Doe' `KNOWS` 'Jane Doe':
```cypher
MERGE (john:Person {name: 'John Doe'})
MERGE (jane:Person {name: 'Jane Doe'})
MERGE (john)-[:KNOWS]->(jane)
RETURN john, jane
```
The true power of `MERGE` is unlocked with `ON CREATE` and `ON MATCH` sub-clauses. These allow you to specify different actions depending on whether `MERGE` found an existing pattern or created a new one. For example, if you `MERGE` a person, you might want to set a `createdDate` property only if the person was newly created, but update a `lastSeen` property if they were matched:
```cypher
MERGE (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
ON CREATE SET p.createdDate = datetime(), p.status = 'active'
ON MATCH SET p.lastSeen = datetime()
RETURN p
```
This query ensures that 'Alice' exists, and then conditionally updates properties based on the `MERGE` outcome. `ON CREATE` and `ON MATCH` are invaluable for managing dynamic data and avoiding redundant operations.

To modify properties or labels of existing nodes and relationships, you use the `SET` clause. `SET` can add new properties, update existing ones, or even add new labels. To update a movie's `releaseYear`:
`MATCH (m:Movie {title: 'New Sci-Fi'}) SET m.releaseYear = 2025 RETURN m`
You can also add multiple properties at once or even replace all properties with a new map:
`MATCH (m:Movie {title: 'New Sci-Fi'}) SET m += {genre: 'Action', rating: 7.5} RETURN m`
To add a new label to a node:
`MATCH (m:Movie {title: 'New Sci-Fi'}) SET m:SciFiMovie RETURN m`
This adds the `SciFiMovie` label to the node, allowing it to be matched by both `Movie` and `SciFiMovie` labels.

Conversely, to remove properties or labels, you use the `REMOVE` clause. `REMOVE` is specifically for properties and labels, not for deleting entire nodes or relationships (which we'll cover in the next chapter). To remove the `rating` property from a movie:
`MATCH (m:Movie {title: 'New Sci-Fi'}) REMOVE m.rating RETURN m`
To remove a label:
`MATCH (m:Movie {title: 'New Sci-Fi'}) REMOVE m:SciFiMovie RETURN m`
It's crucial to distinguish `REMOVE` from `DELETE`. `REMOVE` modifies attributes of an existing graph element, while `DELETE` removes the element itself.

Common mistakes include using `CREATE` when `MERGE` is more appropriate, leading to duplicate nodes or relationships. Always consider if you want to guarantee uniqueness before using `CREATE`. Another mistake is attempting to `REMOVE` a node or relationship directly with `REMOVE`, which will result in a syntax error. Remember `REMOVE` is for properties and labels. When using `SET`, be aware that `SET n = {newProps}` will *replace* all existing properties on node `n` with `newProps`, while `SET n += {newProps}` will *add or update* properties from `newProps` without affecting others. Always verify your `MATCH` clause before executing `SET` or `REMOVE` to ensure you're modifying the correct elements. Data manipulation can be irreversible, so it's a good practice to first `MATCH` and `RETURN` the elements you intend to modify to confirm your target set.

narration.text: Welcome to a crucial chapter in your Neo4j journey! Up until now, we've focused on querying and retrieving data from your graph. But what if you need to build that graph from scratch, or evolve it over time? That's exactly what we'll tackle here. This chapter introduces you to the essential Cypher clauses that allow you to modify your graph data: CREATE, MERGE, SET, and REMOVE. These powerful tools are fundamental for building, maintaining, and updating your graph database, enabling it to reflect real-world changes and grow with your needs. By the end of this chapter, you'll be able to confidently add new entities, ensure data uniqueness, update properties, and refine the structure of your graph. Let's dive into how you can take control of your graph's evolution. Creating and Updating Graph Data means learn to build and modify your neo4j graph with core cypher clauses.. In practical terms, mastering cypher's create, merge, set, and remove clauses. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Now that you've become proficient in retrieving data using Cypher's MATCH and RETURN clauses, it's time to expand your capabilities to actively change and grow your graph. A graph database isn't static; it's a living, evolving representation of your data, and being able to modify it is fundamental to its utility. This chapter introduces you to the essential Cypher clauses for data manipulation: CREATE, MERGE, SET, and REMOVE. Think of these as your primary toolkit for building new connections, adding new entities, updating existing information, and refining your graph's structure. Each clause serves a distinct purpose, and understanding when and how to use them will empower you to build dynamic, accurate, and robust graph applications. We'll explore each one in detail, starting with the most basic operation: adding new elements to your graph. Module 3›Chapter 2›Evolving Your Graph Database
Core Concept

Evolving Your Graph Database

Transitioning from data retrieval to active graph modification.

Why Modify?

Graphs are living data models. Modification allows them to reflect real-world changes, add new insights, and grow over time.

The Core Toolkit

Cypher provides specific clauses: CREATE, MERGE, SET, and REMOVE, each with a distinct role in data manipulation.

Beyond Retrieval

Moving past just reading data, you'll gain the power to build and shape the graph's structure and content.

Cypher Data Manipulation Flow
CREATEAdd new nodes & relationships
MERGEMatch or create idempotently
SETUpdate properties & labels
REMOVEDelete properties & labels

narration.text: The CREATE clause is your entry point for building a graph from scratch or expanding an existing one. It's straightforward: you use it to add entirely new nodes and relationships to your database. When creating a node, you define its label or labels, which categorize it within your graph, and you can assign initial properties, which are key-value pairs describing its attributes. For example, you might create a 'Person' node with a name and a birth year. The beauty of CREATE is its simplicity for direct additions. You can also use CREATE to establish relationships between nodes, whether those nodes already exist or are being created in the same query. This allows you to define the connections that are the very essence of a graph. Remember, CREATE always generates new entities, which is a key characteristic we'll explore further. It's the fundamental building block for populating your graph. Introducing CREATE means create always generates new nodes and relationships, even if identical ones exist.. In practical terms, adding new nodes and relationships. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2›Introducing CREATE
Cypher Clause

Introducing CREATE

Adding New Nodes and Relationships to Your Graph

Node Creation

Define labels and initial properties for new nodes. Example: (p:Person {name: 'Jane Doe', born: 1990}).

Relationship Creation

Connect existing or newly created nodes with relationships. Example: (d)-[:DIRECTED]->(m).

Key Characteristic

CREATE always generates new entities, even if identical ones already exist in the graph.

Code Example: Creating Nodes and Relationships
CREATE (p:Person {name: 'Jane Doe', born: 1990})
RETURN p

CREATE (m:Movie {title: 'New Sci-Fi', releaseYear: 2024})
CREATE (d:Person {name: 'Ava Director'})
CREATE (d)-[:DIRECTED]->(m)
RETURN m, d
Key Takeaway

Use CREATE to explicitly add new nodes and relationships, defining their labels and initial properties.

screens.subtitle: When CREATE Might Not Be Enough

narration.text: While the CREATE clause is excellent for adding new, distinct entities, it comes with an important caveat: it will always create new entities, even if identical nodes or relationships already exist in your graph. This behavior can lead to unintended duplicate data if not managed carefully. Imagine you're importing data from multiple sources, and some entries might overlap. If you simply use CREATE for every entry, you could end up with multiple 'Person' nodes for the same individual, or several identical 'Movie' nodes. This not only bloats your database but also compromises data integrity, making queries less reliable and analysis more complex. Understanding this potential for duplication is crucial, as it highlights a common pitfall and sets the stage for why other clauses, like MERGE, are so vital for robust graph management. Always consider if uniqueness is a requirement before defaulting to CREATE. The Risk of Duplicates with CREATE means create does not check for existing data, potentially leading to redundant nodes and relationships.. In practical terms, when create might not be enough. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Unintended Duplication
keyIdea.text: CREATE does not check for existing data, potentially leading to redundant nodes and relationships.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2›Risk of Duplicates
Important Consideration

The Risk of Duplicates with CREATE

Understanding when CREATE can lead to redundant data.

Always New

CREATE's fundamental behavior is to generate a new graph entity every time it's executed, regardless of existing data.

Data Integrity Risk

Duplicate nodes or relationships can compromise data accuracy, lead to inconsistent query results, and increase storage overhead.

Common Scenario

Importing data from external sources without uniqueness checks often results in unwanted duplicates if only CREATE is used.

Code Example: Accidental Duplication
CREATE (p:Person {name: 'John Doe'})
RETURN p
// Output: (p {name: 'John Doe'}) - new node created

CREATE (p:Person {name: 'John Doe'})
RETURN p
// Output: (p {name: 'John Doe'}) - ANOTHER new node created!
// Now you have two 'John Doe' nodes.
Common Mistake

Using CREATE when you intend to ensure a node or relationship exists only once can lead to significant data quality issues.

screens.title: Introducing MERGE
screens.subtitle: Matching or Creating Graph Patterns Idempotently

narration.text: This is where the MERGE clause becomes incredibly powerful, addressing the duplication issues we just discussed. MERGE is designed for idempotent operations, meaning you can apply it multiple times without changing the result beyond the initial application. It works by attempting to match a specified pattern in the graph. If the pattern already exists, MERGE will find and return it. If it doesn't exist, MERGE will create it. This 'match or create' behavior is invaluable for ensuring data uniqueness and preventing redundant entries. For instance, if you want to ensure a 'Person' node with a specific name exists, but only create it if it's not already there, MERGE is your go-to. It simplifies your logic by handling both scenarios in a single, elegant clause, making your graph data more consistent and reliable. This is a cornerstone of robust graph data management. Introducing MERGE means merge either matches an existing pattern or creates it, ensuring uniqueness and preventing duplicates.. In practical terms, matching or creating graph patterns idempotently. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Idempotent Operations
keyIdea.text: MERGE either matches an existing pattern or creates it, ensuring uniqueness and preventing duplicates.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2›Introducing MERGE
Cypher Clause

Introducing MERGE

Matching or Creating Graph Patterns Idempotently

Idempotent Behavior

MERGE ensures that an operation can be repeated without causing unintended side effects or creating duplicates.

Match or Create

If the specified pattern exists, it's matched. If not, it's created. This prevents redundant data.

Ensuring Uniqueness

Ideal for scenarios where you need to guarantee that a node or relationship exists only once based on its properties.

Code Example: Merging a Node
MERGE (p:Person {name: 'John Doe'})
RETURN p
// If 'John Doe' exists, it's returned.
// If not, a new 'John Doe' node is created and returned.

MERGE (p:Person {name: 'John Doe'})
RETURN p
// Running again returns the SAME 'John Doe' node. No duplicate.
Key Takeaway

Use MERGE when you want to ensure a pattern exists, creating it only if it's not already present.

narration.text: The power of MERGE extends beyond just nodes; it's equally effective for managing relationships idempotently. Just as with nodes, you can use MERGE to ensure that a specific relationship pattern exists between two nodes, creating it only if it doesn't already. This is incredibly useful for maintaining the integrity of your graph's connections. For example, if you want to ensure that 'John Doe' KNOWS 'Jane Doe', you can use MERGE for both the individuals and their relationship. This prevents the creation of duplicate 'KNOWS' relationships if that connection already exists. It's a robust way to model interactions and associations without cluttering your graph with redundant edges. By combining MERGE for both nodes and relationships, you can construct complex graph patterns with confidence, knowing that your data remains clean and unique. This approach is fundamental for building reliable and scalable graph applications. Idempotent Relationships with MERGE means merge can be used to ensure a specific relationship pattern exists, preventing duplicate connections.. In practical terms, ensuring unique connections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Unique Relationships
keyIdea.text: MERGE can be used to ensure a specific relationship pattern exists, preventing duplicate connections.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2›MERGE for Relationships
Advanced MERGE

Idempotent Relationships with MERGE

Ensuring Unique Connections Between Nodes

Pattern Matching

MERGE attempts to find the entire relationship pattern, including the start node, end node, and relationship type.

Preventing Duplicate Edges

If the relationship already exists, it's matched. If not, it's created, ensuring only one of that specific connection.

Complex Graph Building

Allows for the robust construction of interconnected graph structures without worrying about redundant links.

Code Example: Merging Nodes and Relationships
MERGE (john:Person {name: 'John Doe'})
MERGE (jane:Person {name: 'Jane Doe'})
MERGE (john)-[:KNOWS]->(jane)
RETURN john, jane
Key Takeaway

Use MERGE for relationships to ensure unique connections, often combined with MERGE for the nodes themselves.

screens.title: Dynamic Actions with ON CREATE and ON MATCH
screens.subtitle: Tailoring Behavior Based on MERGE Outcome

narration.text: The true power of MERGE is unlocked with its sub-clauses: ON CREATE and ON MATCH. These allow you to specify different actions depending on whether MERGE found an existing pattern or had to create a new one. This conditional logic is incredibly valuable for managing dynamic data. For example, if you MERGE a person, you might want to set a 'createdDate' property only if that person was newly created, capturing when they first appeared in your graph. Conversely, if the person was merely matched because they already existed, you might want to update a 'lastSeen' property to track their most recent interaction. These sub-clauses provide fine-grained control over your data manipulation, allowing you to implement sophisticated logic within a single Cypher query. They are invaluable for maintaining audit trails, managing user activity, or handling complex data synchronization scenarios, making your graph operations much more intelligent and efficient. Dynamic Actions with ON CREATE and ON MATCH means on create and on match allow specific actions based on whether merge created or found a pattern.. In practical terms, tailoring behavior based on merge outcome. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Conditional Property Updates
keyIdea.text: ON CREATE and ON MATCH allow specific actions based on whether MERGE created or found a pattern.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2›ON CREATE / ON MATCH
Conditional Logic

Dynamic Actions with ON CREATE and ON MATCH

Tailoring Behavior Based on MERGE Outcome

ON CREATE

Executes statements only if the MERGE clause created a new node or relationship. Ideal for initial property settings.

ON MATCH

Executes statements only if the MERGE clause found an existing node or relationship. Useful for updating timestamps or counters.

Dynamic Data Management

Enables sophisticated logic for managing user activity, audit trails, and data synchronization within a single query.

Code Example: Conditional Property Updates
MERGE (p:Person {name: 'Alice'})
ON CREATE SET p.createdDate = datetime(), p.status = 'active'
ON MATCH SET p.lastSeen = datetime()
RETURN p
Key Takeaway

Use ON CREATE and ON MATCH with MERGE to apply different property updates based on whether an entity was created or matched.

narration.text: Once nodes and relationships exist in your graph, you'll often need to modify their attributes. This is where the SET clause comes into play. SET is your primary tool for adding new properties, updating existing ones, or even attaching new labels to nodes and relationships. For instance, if a movie's release year changes, you can use SET to update that specific property. It's incredibly flexible: you can update a single property, add multiple properties at once, or even replace all properties with a new map of values. Furthermore, SET allows you to add new labels to a node, effectively categorizing it in additional ways without altering its existing labels. This capability is vital for enriching your graph data over time, adapting to new information, and refining your data model as your understanding of the domain evolves. SET is a cornerstone for maintaining a dynamic and accurate graph. Introducing SET means set adds new properties, updates existing ones, and attaches new labels to graph elements.. In practical terms, updating graph element attributes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Flexible Attribute Modification
keyIdea.text: SET adds new properties, updates existing ones, and attaches new labels to graph elements.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2›Introducing SET
Cypher Clause

Introducing SET

Updating Properties and Labels on Existing Graph Elements

Property Updates

Modify the value of an existing property or add a new property to a node or relationship.

Label Addition

Attach one or more new labels to a node, enhancing its categorization without removing existing ones.

Dynamic Data Enrichment

Essential for evolving your graph's schema and enriching data as new information becomes available.

Code Example: Updating a Property
MATCH (m:Movie {title: 'New Sci-Fi'})
SET m.releaseYear = 2025
RETURN m
Key Takeaway

Use SET to precisely modify properties and add labels to existing nodes and relationships.

narration.text: The SET clause offers even more flexibility for property management. Beyond updating a single property, you can use the plus equals operator to add multiple new properties or update existing ones from a map, without affecting other properties on the node or relationship. This is a powerful way to merge property sets. For example, you can add a 'genre' and 'rating' to a movie simultaneously. It's important to distinguish this from SET n equals open curly brace new Props close curly brace, which would replace *all* existing properties. Additionally, SET allows you to add multiple labels to a node. This means a node can belong to several categories, enabling more nuanced queries and data modeling. For instance, a 'Movie' node could also be labeled 'SciFiMovie' and 'ActionFilm'. These advanced SET techniques provide granular control over your graph's schema and data, allowing for complex and efficient updates. Understanding these nuances is key to mastering graph data manipulation. Flexible Property and Label Updates means use set += for merging properties and set :label for adding multiple labels to nodes.. In practical terms, using += and adding multiple labels. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Advanced SET Operations
keyIdea.text: Use SET += for merging properties and SET :Label for adding multiple labels to nodes.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2›Flexible SET Updates
SET Techniques

Flexible Property and Label Updates

Leveraging += for properties and adding multiple labels.

Merging Properties (+=)

Use SET n += {map} to add new properties or update existing ones from a map without removing others.

Replacing All Properties

Be cautious: SET n = {map} will replace ALL existing properties on n with the new map.

Adding New Labels

Simply use SET n:NewLabel to add a new label to a node, allowing for multi-categorization.

Code Example: Merging Properties and Adding Labels
MATCH (m:Movie {title: 'New Sci-Fi'})
SET m += {genre: 'Action', rating: 7.5}
RETURN m

MATCH (m:Movie {title: 'New Sci-Fi'})
SET m:SciFiMovie
RETURN m
Key Takeaway

Use SET += for partial property updates and SET :Label for adding new labels to nodes.

narration.text: Just as you can add and update properties and labels, you also need the ability to remove them. This is the purpose of the REMOVE clause. REMOVE is specifically designed to delete properties or remove labels from existing nodes and relationships. It's important to understand that REMOVE modifies attributes of an existing graph element; it does not delete the element itself. For example, if a movie's 'rating' property is no longer relevant, you can use REMOVE to delete it. Similarly, if a node was incorrectly labeled or no longer fits a certain category, you can remove a specific label from it. This allows for precise cleanup and refinement of your graph's data model without affecting the core entities. It's a crucial tool for maintaining data quality and adapting your graph schema as requirements change. Remember, REMOVE is about attributes, not about deleting entire nodes or relationships. Introducing REMOVE means remove deletes specific properties or removes labels from nodes and relationships, not the elements themselves.. In practical terms, cleaning up graph element attributes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Attribute Deletion
keyIdea.text: REMOVE deletes specific properties or removes labels from nodes and relationships, not the elements themselves.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 2›Introducing REMOVE
Cypher Clause

Introducing REMOVE

Cleaning Up Graph Element Attributes

Property Removal

Delete a specific property from a node or relationship. Example: REMOVE m.rating.

Label Removal

Remove a specific label from a node. Example: REMOVE m:SciFiMovie.

Attribute-Specific

REMOVE targets properties and labels only; it does not delete entire nodes or relationships.

Code Example: Removing a Property
MATCH (m:Movie {title: 'New Sci-Fi'})
REMOVE m.rating
RETURN m
Key Takeaway

Use REMOVE to precisely delete properties or labels, ensuring your graph data remains clean and relevant.

narration.text: It's crucial to distinguish REMOVE from DELETE. While REMOVE is for properties and labels, DELETE is used to remove entire nodes and relationships from the graph. Attempting to REMOVE a node or relationship directly will result in a syntax error. This distinction is a common area of confusion and a significant pitfall. Another frequent mistake is using CREATE when MERGE is more appropriate, leading to duplicate data. Always ask yourself: do I want to guarantee uniqueness, or do I always want a new entity? When using SET, be aware that SET n equals open curly brace new Props close curly brace will replace all existing properties, while SET n plus equals open curly brace new Props close curly brace will only add or update. Always verify your MATCH clause before executing any modification query to ensure you're targeting the correct elements. Data manipulation can be irreversible, so it's a good practice to first MATCH and RETURN the elements you intend to modify to confirm your target set. These best practices will help you avoid costly errors and maintain a healthy graph.

keyIdea.title: Precision in Deletion
keyIdea.text: REMOVE targets attributes, DELETE targets elements. Understand the difference to avoid data loss.

Best Practices

REMOVE vs. DELETE & Common Pitfalls

Avoiding Data Manipulation Mistakes for a Healthy Graph

REMOVE vs. DELETE

REMOVE is for properties and labels. DELETE (covered later) is for entire nodes and relationships.

CREATE vs. MERGE

Use MERGE for idempotent operations to prevent duplicates; use CREATE only when new entities are always desired.

SET Property Replacement

SET n = {map} replaces all properties. Use SET n += {map} to add/update properties without removing others.

Code Example: Common Mistake - REMOVE Node
MATCH (p:Person {name: 'John Doe'})
REMOVE p
// Syntax Error! REMOVE cannot delete nodes.
// Use DELETE for nodes and relationships.
Key Takeaway

Always confirm your target elements with MATCH and RETURN before modifying, and understand the specific function of each clause.

narration.text: Let's recap the essential Cypher clauses we've covered for creating and updating graph data. First, the CREATE clause is your fundamental tool for adding brand new nodes and relationships to your graph. Remember, it always creates new entities, which is important to keep in mind to avoid duplicates. Next, we explored the MERGE clause, a powerful idempotent operation that either matches an existing pattern in the graph or creates it if it doesn't already exist. This is your go-to for ensuring uniqueness and preventing redundant data. Finally, we looked at the ON CREATE sub-clause, which allows you to execute specific actions, like setting initial properties, only when MERGE results in the creation of a new pattern. These three clauses form the backbone of building and maintaining a clean, evolving graph database.
